talks.title: 0x0F: Jesper Larsson - RCE and the Full Cluster Breach
talks.teaser: Reviews 0x0F: Jesper Larsson - RCE and the Full Cluster Breach and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a freelance penetration tester, had planned to present an attack chain against a Kubernetes-hosted authentication provider used by banks, but shifted focus to post-exploitation once the vulnerable code was easy to find. The entry point was a user-controllable expression language value that the web application evaluated through a class in its codebase. That gave code execution inside an Alpine-based pod, which was turned into a reverse shell.

From the pod, the attack continued with curl-downloaded kubectl and cloud CLIs. The default service account token carried extra permissions that exposed namespace secrets, and config maps held production credentials readable by everyone in the namespace. On Google Kubernetes Engine, a node identity could be obtained by having the cluster sign a certificate request, which the speaker said is enabled by default unless shielded nodes are used. A privileged pod then reached the node's filesystem, and impersonating the Helm Tiller deployment service yielded a cluster administrator token. Separately, a server-side request forgery against an EC2 instance read user data containing secrets, and a Windows example showed startup logic adding a user to the local administrators group.

The speaker argued that teams should know what they deploy, since templates and quick fixes leave secrets behind. Practical steps included not mounting default service account tokens, keeping credentials out of config maps, scrubbing user data after deployment, enabling shielded nodes, retiring Tiller, and linting infrastructure code. Monitoring application behavior and egress traffic was also recommended to spot unexpected outbound shells or tool installs.

talks.title: 0x0F: Ilan Sokol & Eran Ayalon
talks.teaser: Outlines 0x0F: Ilan Sokol & Eran Ayalon - Essential principles in container internals and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary: Cybereason researchers Elaine Sokol and Eran Ayalon explain Linux container internals—namespaces, cgroups, seccomp, and capability bitmasks—then demonstrate real escapes abusing CAP_SYS_MODULE and CAP_SYS_PTRACE. Live demos load a malicious kernel module via call_usermodehelper for root reverse shells and attach GDB to host processes when pid=host and cap_add leak dangerous rights. They map findings to MITRE escape-to-host, cite TeamTNT campaigns and risky GitHub compose files, and recommend dropping all capabilities before adding minimal sets, avoiding privileged pods, and enforcing seccomp-BPF profiles per syscall.

talks.title: 0x0F: Julia Zdunczyk - How to Break into Organizations with Style
talks.teaser: See how card scans and weak configurations can open doors, and learn practical ways to make access systems harder to misuse.
talks.summary: The speaker explains how RFID access cards and readers work, then demonstrates ways to capture or reuse card identifiers, exploit weak configurations, and relay communication between a card and a reader. A red-team assessment example shows how observation, card scans, and testing identifiers led to access to a server room. Attendees learn signs of attempted card scans and defenses such as stronger card configurations, PIN checks, employee awareness, and access logging.

talks.title: 0x0F: Mikael Simovits - Flipper Zero - Zero Trust or Beware of Geeks bearing gifts
talks.teaser: Discusses 0x0F: Mikael Simovits - Flipper Zero - Zero Trust or Beware of Geeks bearing gifts and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether the Flipper Zero, a popular handheld tool for copying and emulating access cards and radio signals, can be trusted. The speaker treats it as a threat intelligence survey built on two questions: whether foreign intelligence services could be linked to the product, and whether it collects data from its users. He argues the hardware adds little new technically; its appeal is simplicity. He also reviews controversies over account blocks, customs seizures and retail bans in several countries.

The research gathered about 80 sources, including Russian and Western media, company pages, interviews, blogs and social media, and rated each source's reliability and the consistency of its claims. The speaker traces the developer ties to a US registered mailbox company and a network of Russian firms and a hackspace. He describes links between key figures and a company whose founder was placed on a US sanctions list, and he judges one founder's earlier online project and later actions as questionable. On telemetry, the desktop updater sent empty requests, while the Android app included a crash-reporting library and a custom metrics library. Some telemetry was seen, a unique user ID and an IP address, though the metrics framework appeared largely unused.

The speaker rates the chance of a link to Russian intelligence as roughly even and sees data harvesting as a realistic future risk, especially if sharing features are added or the open-source project is compromised. Practical indicators include traffic to the vendor's domains and endpoint detection alerts when devices are charged through corporate PCs. He concludes that the tool is competent, but that users should be cautious given the geopolitical situation.

talks.title: 0x0F: STÖK - Weaponizing Plain Text: ANSI Escape Sequences as a Forensic Nightmare
talks.teaser: Reviews 0x0F: STÖK - Weaponizing Plain Text: ANSI Escape Sequences as a Forensic Nightmare and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary: STÖK revives dormant ANSI and OSC escape-sequence abuse for incident responders who trust exported logs and terminal tailing. After a fictional ransomware banner inside a centralized log export, the talk maps CSI color codes, bell characters, and terminal-specific features across Docker Desktop, VS Code, iTerm, Windows Terminal, and cloud SSH consoles. Live Docker logging demos show silent cursor injection and clickable hyperlinks that chain into calc popups, DNS callbacks via SSH or OSC7 working-directory reporting, inline Sixel images, and clipboard polyglots that paste shell commands after social-engineered warnings. Historical title-bar writebacks are dismissed as patched, while fresh RCE paths leverage Kitty file-transfer prompts, VS Code shell-integration command lines, and iTerm2 device-control status strings replayed through vulnerable middleware. Mitigations emphasize log sanitization on write, not blaming analysts for catting untrusted CSV or error logs that remain verbose at HTTP 500.

talks.title: 0x0F: Amit Dori
talks.teaser: Map system components and communication paths to focus security research on the attack surfaces that matter.
talks.summary: The speaker explains how to use threat modeling across an entire system to guide security research before code review or fuzzing begins. Through automotive and virtualization examples, attendees learn to map components and communication paths iteratively, focus on attack surfaces that match organizational priorities, and document risks and assumptions to inform mitigations.
